details:
**"Death, be not proud"**
Donne's most famous sonnet (Holy Sonnet X), an address to Death personified. It denies that Death is "mighty and dreadful," calls it a "slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men," notes that "poppy or charms can make us sleep as well" and asks "why swell'st thou then?" It ends: "One short sleep past, we wake eternally, / And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die."

**Holy Sonnets**
Donne's group of nineteen religious sonnets, also called the Divine Meditations, written after his turn from love poetry to devotion; he later became an Anglican priest and Dean of St. Paul's. Other entries include "This is my play's last scene," "If poisonous minerals" (which asks why, if "lecherous goats" and "serpents envious" cannot be damned, he should be), and the first sonnet, which asks God to "like adamant draw mine iron heart."

**"Batter my heart, three-person'd God"**
Holy Sonnet XIV, which uses violent imagery to ask the Trinity to overpower the speaker: "break, blow, burn, and make me new." He compares himself to "an usurp'd town to another due" and says he is "betroth'd unto your enemy," and the poem ends with the paradox that he will never be "chaste, except you ravish me."

**"A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning"**
A poem in which the speaker tells his beloved not to grieve during his journey away. It opens "As virtuous men pass mildly away," urges "let us melt, and make no noise," and contrasts their love with "dull sublunary lovers' love." Its most famous metaphysical conceit compares their souls to "stiff twin compasses": "Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun." Adrienne Rich borrowed its title for her own poem.

**"The Flea"**
A witty seduction poem in which the speaker points to a flea that "sucked me first, and now sucks thee," so that "our two bloods mingled be," arguing that sex would be no greater sin. When the woman kills it, he asks if she has "purpled thy nail in blood of innocence."

**"The Canonization"**
A love poem that opens "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love." The speaker asks "What merchant's ships have my sighs drowned?", notes that "soldiers find wars, and lawyers find out still litigious men," and compares the lovers to the eagle and the dove and the "phoenix riddle." He says that "We'll build in sonnets pretty rooms" and that a "well-wrought urn" suits their ashes, a phrase Cleanth Brooks used to title his landmark New Criticism book The Well-Wrought Urn, which includes "The Heresy of Paraphrase."

**"No man is an island"**
The most famous passage of Meditation XVII in Donne's prose Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, written during a serious illness. It argues that "every man is a piece of the continent" and "any man's death diminishes me," and it ends "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee."

**"I am a little world made cunningly"**
Holy Sonnet V, in which the speaker describes himself as a microcosm of "elements and an angelic sprite" and laments that "black sin" has betrayed "to endless night my world's both parts." He asks to have new seas poured into his eyes so he can drown his world with weeping.

**"To His Mistress Going to Bed"**
An erotic elegy in which the speaker urges his lover to undress, famously comparing her body to a newly discovered land: "O my America! my new-found-land."

**"The Triple Fool"**
A poem whose speaker admits "I am two fools, I know, / For loving, and for saying so / In whining poetry." He hoped that writing verse would ease his grief, as "earth's inward narrow crooked lanes" purge salt from sea water, but when his poems are set to music, he becomes a triple fool.

**Ann More and "Since she whom I loved"**
Donne secretly married Ann More in 1601, which ruined his career for years, and her death in 1617 deeply affected him. Holy Sonnet XVII, "Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt," mourns her. His early biography was written by Izaak Walton.

**The Anniversaries**
Long poems commemorating the death of the young Elizabeth Drury, daughter of Donne's patron. The first, "An Anatomy of the World," mourns the decay of the world and ends that when you know "she's dead," you know "how lame a cripple this world is."

**"The Relic"**
A poem from Songs and Sonnets imagining that when his grave is dug up, someone will find "a bracelet of bright hair about the bone," and the lovers will be worshipped as relics.

**Wit**
Margaret Edson's Pulitzer Prize-winning play about Dr. Vivian Bearing, a Donne scholar dying of ovarian cancer, who reflects on the Holy Sonnets, especially "Death, be not proud," as she faces her own death.

**"The Bait"**
Donne's response to Christopher Marlowe's "The Passionate Shepherd to His Love," beginning with the same line, "Come live with me and be my love," but turning the pastoral into a fishing conceit in which the woman is the bait.
